package_info.package_versions: all published versions (since at least Dec 4, 2023)
package_info.why_malicious: These packages abuse the npm registry by storing and distributing large, non-software media files (movies, video clips, and eBooks), violating the platform's terms of service and threatening the integrity and hygiene of the software supply chain. While not containing traditional malware, their presence constitutes a supply chain risk and potential copyright violation.

execution_context.trigger: import-time (when package is downloaded or inspected)
execution_context.file_location: package root directory (multiple .ts files, e.g., video1.ts, video2.ts)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Stores and delivers large video files (movie clips) as part of the package contents.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Software packages are expected to contain code and necessary assets, not large, unrelated media files. The presence of multi-gigabyte video files is highly anomalous.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm packages contain JavaScript/TypeScript code and small assets, not split movie files.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate packages may include small demo videos or images for documentation, but not full-length movies or pirated content.
key_indicators: Multiple large .ts files in package root
Total package size ~54.5 MB per package
No actual code or software functionality

execution_context.trigger: import-time (when package is downloaded or inspected)
execution_context.file_location: package root directory (JSON files, e.g., comments.json)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Contains time-synced user comments, likely scraped from online video streaming platforms, accompanying the video files.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: JSON files with time-synced comments are not typical for npm packages, especially when not related to any code functionality.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages may include configuration or metadata JSON, but not user comment data for pirated media.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use could be subtitle or comment files for open-source video players, but not in the context of pirated movie distribution.
key_indicators: No code referencing or using these files

attack_chain.action: Attacker uploads multiple npm packages, each containing a segment of a pirated movie (as .ts files) and associated comment data (as JSON).
attack_chain.leads_to: Packages are available for download from npm registry.

attack_chain.action: User (or script) downloads all packages with the 'wlwz-' prefix, reconstructs the full movie from the .ts segments and optionally the comment data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Distribution and consumption of pirated media via npm.

behavioral_signatures: npm packages with no code, only large binary media files
Packages with multiple .ts files and/or large JSON files containing user comments
Unusually large package sizes (e.g., >50 MB) with no software functionality
file_indicators: comments.json or similar large JSON files with time-synced comments
package.json with minimal or no code dependencies
network_indicators: No direct network indicators (malicious activity is in package content, not runtime behavior)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Flag npm packages that contain large binary files (e.g., .ts, .mp4) unrelated to software functionality, especially when package size exceeds typical thresholds and there is no accompanying code. Look for packages with repeated naming patterns (e.g., 'wlwz-*'), and inspect for the presence of media files or unrelated JSON data. Automated scanning for non-code assets and anomalous package size can help detect this abuse.
